title: Hybrid Analysis for Secure MCP Tool Use in LLM Agents

images.desc:
1. Introduction


Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the rapid development of LLM agents that can solve complex real-world tasks by planning, invoking tools, and interacting with external environments (Zhang et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025c; Chang et al., 2026; Mok et al., 2025; OpenClaw, 2026).
To support standardized interaction between agents and external resources, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Anthropic, 2026) has emerged as a de facto standard for tool integration.
However, the same unified interface also introduces a critical security boundary: an untrusted or compromised MCP tool can influence an agent’s decisions and cause harmful side effects in the host environment.
For example, tool poisoning attacks (Labs, 2026b; He et al., 2025b) can manipulate an agent into invoking tools with unsafe arguments or performing unintended actions.
Securing the entire MCP tool invocation lifecycle is therefore essential for deploying LLM agents in real-world applications.


Existing defenses (Xiang et al., 2025; Jing et al., 2025; Tencent Zhuque Lab, 2025; Labs, 2026a; Sha et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2025) for LLM tool use operate primarily on information available at the message level, such as user prompts, conversation histories, tool metadata, tool descriptions, invocation parameters, and textual results.
Although these approaches can identify suspicious instructions or inconsistencies in tool metadata, they generally do not observe the system-level side effects produced during tool execution.
This design leaves a fundamental blind spot: a malicious MCP tool can appear benign in its metadata and returned messages while performing harmful actions at runtime, such as accessing sensitive files, spawning unexpected subprocesses, or communicating with untrusted endpoints.


However, closing this blind spot requires more than directly applying conventional sandboxing or runtime monitoring.
Although sandboxing and runtime monitoring are mature techniques in traditional software security, MCP tool usage protection introduces a distinct semantic gap.
Low-level execution traces alone do not directly reveal whether a behavior is unsafe; the same file access or network request may be benign or suspicious depending on the tool’s declared functionality, input parameters, and the agent’s task context.
An effective MCP defense must therefore connect runtime side effects with the semantic context of the invocation.
This observation motivates a hybrid approach that combines contextual inspection of MCP messages with dynamic analysis of tool execution.


To bridge this gap, we propose a hybrid analysis-based defense framework that serves as an MCP tool usage guard for LLM agents, termed MTGuard.
At a high level, MTGuard is deployed as a separate guard agent that protects the target LLM agent throughout the MCP tool invocation process.
Instead of treating a tool invocation as a static message or treating runtime monitoring as a standalone sandboxing mechanism, MTGuard couples both views throughout the tool use lifecycle.
The static view provides the semantic context needed to understand what the tool is supposed to do, whereas the dynamic view provides execution evidence about what the tool actually does.
This combination enables MTGuard to detect attacks that are invisible to either view alone, especially tool execution hijacking, where the tool call appears benign, but the executed behavior is malicious.


In practice, MTGuard examines tool calling parameters before execution, monitors tool behavior during execution, and audits execution results after completion, consisting of three components: the pre-execution parameter auditor, the in-execution behavioral monitor, and the post-execution result verifier.
This design follows the natural lifecycle of MCP tool invocation, which can be divided into three stages: pre-execution, in-execution, and post-execution.
Correspondingly, the pre-execution auditor and post-execution verifier apply user-defined textual and code safety policies to inspect tool parameters and execution results, respectively.
Depending on the stage at which a violation is detected, MTGuard rejects the invocation, terminates the running tool, or withholds the unsafe result and returns a denial message to the target agent.


For runtime analysis, the behavioral monitor executes each MCP tool within a controlled sandbox and records its system-level behaviors during execution.
To make runtime traces actionable for MCP tool usage safety analysis, the behavioral monitor introduces a novel data structure, termed the tool behavior tree.
Unlike a conventional process tree, which primarily represents parent and child relationships among processes, the tool behavior tree is rooted at an MCP tool invocation and organizes heterogeneous runtime events, including process activities, file operations, and network communications, according to their provenance and execution dependencies.
This representation transforms fragmented low-level audit logs into an interpretable description of tool behavior.
By analyzing the tree together with the tool description, invocation parameters, safety policies, and agent task context, MTGuard can determine whether the tool’s observed behavior is consistent with its declared and intended functionality.
The resulting semantic connection between protocol-level context and execution-level evidence enables MTGuard to detect attacks that are difficult to identify from either source alone.


We evaluate MTGuard in two representative safety-critical LLM agent scenarios derived from the MCP-SafetyBench (Zong et al., 2025), namely browser automation agent (Ning et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Chae et al., 2025) and financial analysis agent (Zhang et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a, 2026a), using multiple backend LLMs under three MCP attack settings.
This setup enables us to examine the effectiveness and efficiency of MTGuard across diverse tasks and adversarial conditions.
Experimental results show that MTGuard consistently improves the security of MCP tool use in real-world LLM agent applications.
Compared with existing baselines (Deng et al., 2026), MTGuard achieves stronger defense performance while incurring low runtime overhead.
Across the evaluated settings, MTGuard detects an average of 48.3% of unsafe MCP tool calls, compared with 8.3% for the evaluated baseline methods.
In the meantime, MTGuard maintains an average false positive rate of 3.7%, indicating limited disruption to benign tool use and the normal functionality of the target LLM agents.
In addition, MTGuard introduces only a modest runtime overhead, with an average additional latency of about 10 seconds in total across the evaluated settings.
Our ablation study further demonstrates the importance of combining multiple analysis stages: the pre-execution-only variant cannot detect attacks whose malicious behavior emerges only during host-side execution, whereas the complete MTGuard consistently provides the strongest protection.


The key contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:




• 

We identify a runtime observability blind spot in existing MCP tool-use defenses and propose MTGuard, a hybrid defense framework that combines protocol-level contextual inspection with dynamic execution analysis.



• 

We design a lifecycle-aware protection architecture consisting of a pre-execution parameter auditor, an in-execution behavioral monitor, and a post-execution result verifier.
We further introduce the tool behavior tree, which organizes heterogeneous system events and their execution dependencies into an interpretable representation of MCP tool behavior.



• 

We conduct extensive experiments in browser automation and financial analysis scenarios across multiple backend LLMs and MCP attack settings.
The results show that MTGuard substantially improves the detection of unsafe tool calls while maintaining a low false-positive rate and moderate runtime overhead.





Figure 1. The overview of MTGuard. It consists of three key components: pre-execution parameter auditor, in-execution behavioral monitor, and post-execution result verifier.

4.2. Defense effectiveness


We first evaluate the attacks against the target LLM agents without defense to verify that they can induce unsafe MCP tool invocations.
The attack success rates are reported in Appendix B.
We then evaluate MTGuard under the same attack settings.
To enable a consistent tool-call-level comparison, the pre-execution auditor, behavioral monitor, and post-execution verifier are invoked at their original positions in the online tool-use pipeline, but their denial decisions do not block tool execution or modify tool results.
Instead, each decision is recorded as a counterfactual enforcement verdict indicating whether the corresponding call would be denied in deployment.
This protocol preserves the complete agent trajectory, allows post-execution behaviors to be collected even when the pre-execution auditor raises an alert, and enables all defenses to be evaluated over the same tool-call traces.
For DR, we include only tool calls whose unsafe behavior is confirmed by the attack-specific evaluator.


For the policy configuration, we enable seven deterministic function rules in the pre-execution parameter auditor.
These rules detect sensitive-file access, dangerous shell commands, SSH persistence, off-task suspicious URLs, shadowed tool names, task and ticker mismatches, and repeated navigation to the same URL, with the repetition threshold set to three.
The function rules are evaluated before LLM-based auditing and immediately produce a denial verdict when a violation is found.
We additionally configure three natural-language policy rules for both the pre- and post-execution LLM auditors.
These rules prohibit task-irrelevant access to credentials, shell initialization files, SSH keys, and privilege probes; reject navigation or fetching of suspicious off-task endpoints; and require tool arguments such as tickers, destinations, and websites to remain consistent with the user task rather than poisoned tool metadata.
The pre-execution auditor evaluates these policies using the task context, tool name, parameter schema, and declared arguments.
The post-execution verifier additionally receives the execution result, tool behavior tree, and DNS events, allowing it to compare the agent-declared invocation with the behavior that was actually executed.
This configuration combines low-cost deterministic detection of known attack signatures with LLM-based semantic analysis of task alignment and declared-versus-actual behavioral consistency.


We compare MTGuard with the TCG and TRI baselines described in the experimental setup.
Table 1 reports the tool-call level DR under the three attack sources.
Across the six agent and model configurations, MTGuard detects 116 of 240 unsafe tool calls, achieving an overall DR of 48.3%.
In comparison, TCG detects 20 unsafe calls and achieves a DR of 8.3%, while TRI does not detect any unsafe calls in the evaluated traces.
The advantage of MTGuard is particularly evident for MCP host-side attacks: it detects 48 of 64 unsafe calls, corresponding to a DR of 75.0%, whereas both baselines achieve 0.0%.
This improvement is primarily attributable to the behavioral monitor and post-execution verifier, which expose the mismatch between the benign agent-declared invocation and the command actually executed by the Tool Call Hook.
In contrast, TCG observes only the original call declaration, while TRI looks for injection-related textual patterns in tool results and therefore cannot capture this runtime substitution.

Defense effectiveness also differs substantially across attack sources.
MTGuard achieves a DR of 100.0% (16/16) against user-side attacks because these attacks produce explicit malicious commands or sensitive-resource accesses that can be recognized from the declared arguments.
For host-side attacks, MTGuard achieves 75.0% (48/64), with its detections concentrated on the Tool Call Hook attacks that produce an explicit declared-versus-actual inconsistency.
The DR is lower for server-side attacks, at 32.5% (52/160).
Many server-side attacks manipulate tool selection, parameters, preferences, or returned values while continuing to invoke legitimate tools through syntactically valid arguments.
Consequently, their execution traces may remain close to normal tool behavior, making them more difficult to identify than explicit command execution or tool-call hijacking.


From the agent-domain perspective, MTGuard achieves an aggregate DR of 52.6% (51/97) for the browser automation agent and 45.5% (65/143) for the financial analysis agent.
The higher overall DR in browser automation is partly explained by server-side attacks involving suspicious URLs, shadowed navigation tools, and repeated navigation patterns, which provide observable signals in tool names, arguments, or network behavior.
In contrast, many attacks in financial analysis alter tickers, preferences, or returned financial values while preserving the expected structure of legitimate Yahoo Finance calls.
Such semantic manipulations may produce plausible arguments and normal-looking runtime traces, making them harder to distinguish from benign financial operations.


FPR. 
We further evaluate whether the defenses incorrectly flag safe MCP tool calls.
As shown in Table 2, MTGuard maintains a relatively low FPR across the evaluated configurations.
Its unweighted average FPR across the six agent and model configurations is 3.7%, compared with 0.3% for TCG and 0.4% for TRI.
Although MTGuard has a higher FPR than the rule-based baselines, it provides substantially broader detection coverage, particularly for server-side and host-side attacks.
The FPR of MTGuard is slightly higher for browser automation, averaging 3.9%, than for financial analysis, which averages 3.4%.
Browser tasks involve longer and more heterogeneous interaction trajectories, including repeated navigation and transitions across external websites.
Some of these benign behaviors may resemble replay or off-task navigation and consequently trigger the corresponding deterministic or semantic checks.


The low overall FPR is supported by the conservative decision principles used in the LLM-based auditors.
In particular, the post-execution verifier adopts an allow-by-default policy for behavior that is consistent with the declared invocation and requires clear evidence of hijacking, task-irrelevant sensitive access, or suspicious network activity before returning a denial.
The structured prompts further require the auditor to examine task alignment, argument integrity, policy compliance, and declared-versus-actual consistency before making its decision.


Figure 2. The time overheads of MTGuard on the LLM agents. (a) The audit duration of the pre-execution parameter auditor. (b) The audit duration of the post-execution result verifier.


Defense overheads. 
To quantify the latency introduced by LLM-based auditing, we measure the duration of each pre-execution and post-execution LLM audit and group the results by agent domain.
As shown in Figure 2, the average pre-execution audit latency is 5.93 seconds for browser automation and 5.68 seconds for financial analysis.
The corresponding post-execution audit latency is 6.74 and 6.40 seconds, respectively.
Thus, when both LLM auditing stages are invoked, they introduce approximately 12.39 seconds of additional latency per tool call.


These measurements include only LLM-based audit latency and exclude the near-zero-cost deterministic function-rule checks, tool execution time, and sandbox or eBPF monitoring costs.
The post-execution verifier is slightly slower because its prompt contains additional execution evidence, including the tool result, behavior tree, and DNS events.
Although the added latency is measurable, it remains bounded and may be acceptable for security-sensitive agent applications.
